analysis.one_liner: Cuts copyright terms to 28 years, renewable once, and retroactively cuts off the largest media companies' existing copyrights.
analysis.headline: The bill died in committee: referred to the House Judiciary Committee in January 2023, it drew zero cosponsors and never received a hearing, markup, or vote before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would shorten copyright protection for new works from the current 'life of the author plus 70 years' to 28 years, renewable for one additional 28-year term. It would also apply retroactively to existing copyrights owned by any motion picture or arts-and-entertainment company worth more than $150 billion — a line that in practice captures only the very largest media conglomerates. Works would enter the public domain far sooner, meaning anyone could freely republish, adapt, or remix them without paying a license fee.
analysis.who_benefits: The general public: works would become freely available for reuse, adaptation, and republication after 28 or 56 years instead of being locked up for roughly a century. Teachers, libraries, filmmakers, musicians, and small publishers who build on older works would gain access without licensing costs.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Readers, creators, and reusers of older works

how_it_helps.text: Shortens the copyright term for new works to 28 years, renewable once for another 28 years, instead of the current life of the author plus 70 years.
Applies retroactively to existing copyrights owned by media or entertainment companies with a market capitalization above $150 billion, terminating those copyrights on the shortened schedule.
Grants limited continued protection to pre-existing licensees of the affected mega-company copyrights, but only for the shorter of half the remaining license term or 10 years.

analysis.who_pays: Copyright holders. Studios, record labels, book publishers, and individual authors and musicians would see their new works lose protection decades earlier, cutting licensing revenue. The largest media conglomerates would additionally lose their existing catalogs to the public domain.

drawbacks.text: Individual creators lose the most: a novelist or songwriter would see their work enter the public domain within their own lifetime, forfeiting decades of income the current life-plus-70 term provides.

The retroactive provision applies only to entertainment companies worth more than $150 billion rather than to all copyright holders, an arbitrary line drawn at a size very few firms meet, and the shortening would cut off rights in existing works without compensation.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: A shorter, uniform copyright term is a defensible reform that would meaningfully expand the public domain, where the strongest benefit lies. But the bill undercuts its own logic: it imposes the short term on everyone's new works — including individual creators who lose decades of income — while the retroactive provision is aimed solely at a handful of mega-cap media companies rather than applied evenhandedly. A cleaner bill would shorten terms prospectively and treat all owners alike.

outcome.mechanism: Referred to the House Judiciary Committee in January 2023, it sat there without a hearing or vote for the rest of the two-year Congress and never attracted a single cosponsor.

narrative.text: Rep. W. Gregory Steube (R-FL) introduced the bill on January 26, 2023, and it was referred to the House Committee on the Judiciary.
No member of the House, from either party, ever signed on as a cosponsor.
The bill's only actions after introduction were the referral itself; no hearing, markup, committee vote, or floor action ever occurred before the 118th Congress ended.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Major media companies and other long-term copyright holders, who keep the existing life-plus-70 term and their locked-up catalogs; the public gets no expansion of the public domain.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Large media companies and copyright holders

for.name: Rep. W. Gregory Steube
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and remained its only sponsor; no colleague ever joined him.

against.name: House Committee on the Judiciary
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral and took no further action — no hearing, no markup, no committee vote — for the remainder of the Congress.

against.name: House members of both parties
against.what_they_did: None signed on as cosponsors over the bill's two-year life.

sides.party_line_note: The bill drew zero cosponsors from either party and never reached a vote, so no partisan pattern shows up anywhere in the record.

industries.industry: Major media and entertainment conglomerates (companies above $150 billion market cap)
industries.note: The bill would retroactively terminate their existing copyrights — the only retroactive application in the bill — wiping out long-term control of catalogs that generate licensing revenue. Their interest in the current century-long term runs directly against the public's interest in an open public domain.

industries.industry: Studios, record labels, and book publishers below the size threshold
industries.note: They would keep their existing copyrights but see the term on all new works cut from roughly a century to 28 or 56 years, shrinking future licensing income. Their interest in long terms conflicts with the public's interest in works becoming freely usable.

industries.industry: Individual authors, songwriters, and visual artists
industries.note: Their new works would enter the public domain within their lifetimes, ending royalty income decades earlier than current law. Creators' desire for long protection conflicts with the public's interest in free reuse.
